Subject: Introductions: UNOPS and Sweden in Kenya
Body:
Dear Annika, 
My name is Asbjørn Brink, and I am heading the Northern Europe Liaison Office within UNOPS, headquartered in Copenhagen. 
I am writing as I will be in Nairobi from December 2-5 and would greatly appreciate the opportunity to meet with you and your relevant colleagues along with my local UNOPS colleagues in Nairobi (cc this email). 
During our meeting, I would be delighted to explore how UNOPS could further contribute to advancing Sweden’s development aid priorities. Our expertise in project implementation, infrastructure, procurement, and capacity building positions us as a strong partner in achieving shared objectives, particularly in areas such as climate resilience, gender equality, and inclusive economic development.

We would also like to share some recent examples of UNOPS’ impactful work across the African continent. From building climate-resilient infrastructure in vulnerable regions to enhancing access to healthcare and education in underserved communities, our initiatives align closely with Sweden’s focus on poverty reduction and sustainable development.
I would greatly appreciate it if you could please let me know if you are available for a meeting between December 2-5. We look forward to the opportunity to discuss potential synergies and ways we can collaborate to amplify Sweden’s development goals.
Thank you very much in advance for your time and consideration.

All the best,Asbjørn

Today I met, and received the below from WHO. This is a good opportunity but we need to move fast and I am seeking your guidance on how we pull this together with 1 or more MCOs as the potential "anchor" to support development of the proposal (deadline in 9 days) and the project beyond that.

Dear Louise,
 
It was great to see you this morning. As per our discussion please find attached the terms of reference to support the operationalization of the Health Impact Investment Platform (HIIP) ensuring its initial success by focusing on national
 investment plans and work done on Health Emergency Preparedness and Response (HEPR).

 
You may be interested to respond to the proposal as UNOPS to provide support on:

 

1.                  
Establishing a core group at WHO/government level and developing country profiles summarizing the situation and country context;

2.                  
Facilitating development of national investment plans;

3.                  
Outlining a standard approach for developing national investment plans building on earlier experience;

4.                  
Assessing the health financing landscape and recommendations for optimizing health financing;


5.                  
Identifying a package of investable projects in consultation with governments and MDBs.

 
In your proposals can you please provide details of:
 

Your expertise and fit for purpose to support each deliverable
Your proposed team structure, size and composition (including proposed resources and bios)Your financial proposal (based on the existing LTAs, if any) with indicated cost savings and discounts
 
In your response, please use the attached narrative template and budget template.

 
We will evaluate the proposals (both technically and financially) with the relevant technical and regional teams, and make recommendations to be reviewed by the Contracts Review Committee.

 
Should you have question prior the deadline and no later than 28 November COB (CET time), please send them to the team via
WHESPP@who.int.
 
The deadline for receiving completed proposals is Friday, 29 November 2024 COB (CET time),
to the email: WHESPP WHESPP@who.int.
 
All the best,
 
Scott

Dear Munier
Hope all is well with you - I had a good chat with Shible Sahbani this morning and was very happy to hear you are already well connected with him !!
As an ex WHO staff myself of 20 years, I do like to ensure all my UNOPS colleagues are well connected with WHO colleagues and can engage with them usefully (there is a lot of jargon in global public health! ;)   Dr Tedros (WHO DG) met with Jorge 2 weeks ago in Copenhagen, and they discussed our collaboration in health infrastructure, oxygen and emergencies... good timing :) - and I hear Jorge is coming your way soon :) 
I was happy to hear there seems to be quite a lot of health infrastructure being prioritised, with UNOPS potentially being considered for the rehabilitation of 10 secondary level hospitals (with the primary health hospital infrastructure going to UNICEF)
Shible also mentioned Medical Oxygen support is desperately needed - we have implemented a number of excellent projects in Zambia and Bangladesh, financed by the Global Fund. I have reached out to the Fund Portfolio Manager for Sudan, and will revert to you when he responds. 
I also understand WHO wishes to convert its temporary contract holders (SSAs) potentially to ICAs. We already have a global agreement with WHO on HR, so this should be easy to do @Lorraine ANABTAWI  manages this Agreement.
Shible also mentioned an interest in our Access to health model in Myanmar, the multi donor fund, managed by UNOPS with a consortium of NGOS delivering basic health services in non-state controlled areas. Happy to discuss this further with you / support if I can.
Looking forward to hearing from you in due course - perhaps time for a quick catch up ?!
Warmest greetings from GenevaBest wishes Louise

Body:
Kære Magnus
Jeg rækker ud til dig som opfølgning på dialog med dine kolleger i Oslo, da jeg snart skal på mission til Østafrika med henblik på at se nogle af de projekter, som vi i UNOPS gennemfører på vegne af partnere. I den forbindelse ville jeg også meget gerne mødes med repræsentanter for nordiske partnere med henblik på at drøfte evt. samarbejdsmuligheder - især som opfølgning på Norges nye Afrikastrategi. 
Jeg vil være i Nairobi i perioden 2-5 december og ville meget gerne mødes med dig og evt. dine relevante kolleger på et tidspunkt, som kunne passe dig. 
Formålet med mødet vil bl.a. være opfølgning på mødet mellem vores regionale afrikadirektørs (Dalila) møde med den norske ambassadør for et par måneder siden, hvor vi kunne se på evt. synergier mellem Norges Afrikastrategi, prioriteter, og UNOPS' arbejde på det afrikanske kontinent. 
Vi har bl.a. bemærket, at den nye norske afrikastrategi understreget behovet for en stærk forpligtelse til at understøtte bæredygtig udvikling, uddannelse og sundhed, menneskerettigheder og sikkerhed i de afrikanske samfund. I UNOPS gennemfører vi pt. adskillige projekter i Afrika som er på linje med norske prioriteter, såsom opbygning af bæredygtig energiinfrastruktur, vandforsyning, kvinderettigheder, opførelse af skoler mv. 
Jeg ville derfor sætte stor pris på, om du og evt. dine relevante kolleger havde mulighed for at mødes på et tidspunkt, som passer dig i perioden 2-5 december. Lad mig meget gerne vide hvornår det kunne passe dig. 
På forhånd mange tak! 
PS - til din orientering har jeg også forsøgt at sende en mail adresseret til din kollega Camilla Ravnsborg Aschjem - dog uden held, da jeg ikke har hendes direkte e-mail (vedlagt korrespondance). 
Jeg ser meget frem til at høre fra dig. 
MvhAsbjørn

Dear Asbjørn,
 
I hope this message finds you well. I wanted to thank you once again for our great conversation last week, and I’m sending you warm greetings from Nepal.
 
I had a productive discussion with Sidsel, CEO of the LEGO Foundation. She plans for us to attend their board meeting either in March or May, with March being
 the more likely option, though this depends on whether Chairman Thomas is able to attend in person. Before then, Sidsel will coordinate with Thomas to determine the scale of the donation we should pursue—whether it will be for 5, 10, or 20 schools, which would
 amount to between 3 and 12 million USD.
 
As agreed, I’ve summarized the key points from our conversation below, which we can use as a foundation for our ongoing work together.
 
---------oooOooo--------
 
HPF is the program lead in relation to LEGO.
We will establish an overarching steering committee, where HPF, LEGO, and UNOPS will all be represented.
 
UNOPS will be responsible for procurement related to construction and
 materials for libraries, etc.
Additionally, we will set up a
Technical Committee, where HPF and UNOPS will review construction costings, the process for selection of contractors, and UNOPS will help build the capacity of HPF and the local community.
 
---------oooOooo--------
 
The next step is for you, Asbjørn, and the UNOPS team to meet with the HPF Kenya Country Director in Nairobi at the start of December to discuss the local collaboration
 in more detail.
 
I will keep you informed about developments with LEGO, and we will after your Kenya trip discuss collaboration documents and costs.
😊
 
Please do let me know if I’ve missed anything, or if there is anything we should clarify further at this stage.
 
I look forward to hearing how your discussions in Kenya are progressing.
 
Best wishes,

Dear Jakob


 


Thank you for your response and valuable considerations on the way forward. 


 


We are consulting a wider group of our legal experts and will provide additional written elaborated explanations in Ukrainian on the 4 remaining disagreements in the draft legal
 agreement with CCD (as an agreement with the contractor has been reached). Based on that, Teressa and Svitlana will meet with the CCD again on Tuesday next week to make another attempt to reach an agreement. Following this meeting we will consult with you
 again on the way forward. 


 


We are very conscious of the fact that the CCD by the end of the day will be the formal recipient of the final reconstructed Arkas High School - and therefore has to be closely
 involved in the entire process, taking into account all of their input, technical advice, requests, etc. It is therefore crucial for the success of the reconstruction project that all parties (Denmark as the donor, UNOPS as the project manager, the contractor(s)
 and the CCD as the final recipient) are aligned. To ensure this we have for example incorporated legally binding requirements of monthly CCD inspections of the work. 


 


We are flagging the issues on contractual disagreements to you now, as the negotiations with the contractor and the CCD have been ongoing for a long time with more than 20 iterations
 at working level with the CCD alone. If Teressa and Svitlana are not able to reach a workable solution with the CCD next week at their level, I believe that we need to escalate the matter. Otherwise I fear that too much time will be lost without substantive progress. 


 


We may therefore need to call upon your help to escalate the matter with the local Ukrainian authorities to ensure that an amicable solution is reached with an agreement without
 potential conflicts of interests and a minimized risk assessment. 


 


As outlined in Teressa's document (attached here for ease of reference), the contractor was selected after a public tender process approved by CCD. The contractor has requested
 that all communication between the contractor and CCD happens via UNOPS as the project manager - which would ensure arms length and avoid potential conflicts of interests, etc. 


 


To specify the outstanding points, I have reiterated them below: 




CCD requests that UNOPS can only pay the contractor upon approval from CCD




would be a violation of UN financial rules and regulations
UNOPS would in practice lose control over the project
would severely increase financial risk assessment



CCF requests the right to terminate the agreement with the contractor unilaterally with a notice period of 30 days




unacceptable to contractor
could create unfortunate conflicts of interests between contractor and CCD
in violation with UN financial rules and regulations as UNOPS is the entity contracting 
UNOPS would in practice lose control over the project



CCD is to be the technical author and supervisor 



while CCD certainly should provide technical advice, requests, input, observations and must be consulted regularly (see agreement on monthly basis), the technical
supervision of the reconstruction project has to be done by UNOPS as the project manager and as the responsible entity for ensuring the quality of the final product



Contractor has to eliminate defects after the first 12 months of finalising the project




the defects notification period that can be accepted by UNOPS is 12 months which is standard for these types of infrastructure reconstruction projects
during the first 12 months after finalising the reconstruction, flaws, etc. can be notified to UNOPS and we will make sure that it is dealt with within the 12 months period. For this reason we will only make the final payments to the contractor(s) after the
 12 months defects notification period. 



We would be very happy to jump on a call at your convenience to elaborate on the matter. Otherwise I would suggest that we touch base during next week. 


 


We remain as always at your entire disposal for any comments, questions, requests or otherwise. 


 


All the best,


Asbjørn

Body:
Dear Sune
Thank you for your review and always rapid responses. 
In the attached we have accepted the non-substantial track changes for other paragraphs than 5 and 8 to make it easier to read. 
With regards to paragraph 5, we are concerned that using the term ‘promptly’ can be interpreted to mean an almost immediate notification, which in some cases may not be possible depending on a number of factors (eg. if the awareness came via whistleblowing process or via audit, time to look into its credibility, prioritisation of resources, etc.). We would therefore propose to remove the timing requirement and leave it as “UNOPS shall notify“. - Would that be acceptable?
With regards to paragraph 8 our concern is that the agreement can be interpreted to mean that Denmark has the right to question the independent investigations or operations of our independent Investigations and Audit Group (IAIG), which we cannot agree to. In this respect we would like to make you aware of our operational directives regarding investigations (see attached OD.ED.2022.01). See especially section 6: Accountabilities of IAIG Personnel for further background as to IAIG’s role and accountability. 
With UNOIOS, it would appear to us that Denmark already has some arrangements between your auditors and UNOIOS auditors to be able to agree to the language. With some donors, our IAIG has an established relationship with its counterpart on the donor’s side memorialized through an MoU or within a template agreement for example. 
While we do not (yet) have any such MoU or template agreement between UNOPS and Denmark - I believe that it would be useful to aim for such an established relationship to be solidified in a potential upcoming MoU / template. However, given the timing of this engagement I do not think that it would be possible to finalise such an MoU / template in time. We will however commit to incorporate language on such a collaboration in an MoU / template - and we would also commit to amend any past engagements once such an MoU / template has been established between UNOPS and Denmark. 
- Would that be acceptable?
Thank you in advance. 
All the best,Elene and Asbjørn

Subject: Re: SFA incident notification - urgent call
Body:
Dear Gamila, 
I hope this message finds you both well.  As you know, UNOPS cannot comply with the World Bank's ESS reporting requirements for SEA incidents due to our adherence to a different UN reporting mechanism and our inability to commit to the timelines outlined in the Annex 1 of the new SFA template. Our process keeps SEA incident reports strictly confidential until they are disclosed to UN country leadership and the Secretary General's Office, after which basic information becomes publicly available to donors. This discrepancy has become a sticking point in our discussions. 
We have invested some effort internally, working closely with our Internal Audit and Investigation Group, to develop a proposal we hope will address your concerns while taking into account our limitations. This proposal, which consists of the following steps, is inspired a solution considered by other UN agencies: 
1) SEA cases are reported by the Country Office (CO) to IAIG.2) IAIG will report all cases (received through the CO and directly) to the SG through the iTracker.3) IAIG will complete the early incident reporting form (as required by OSCEA). This form contains highly confidential information (allegations, name and DOB of victim).4) The CO will share the allegation number from the iTracker with GRS to inform them of the allegations and allow them to track the case's progress5) The CO will respond to GRS on any questions related to mitigating measures and operational matters6) IAIG will respond to GRS on follow-up high-level investigative questions. Regarding the timelines specified in Annex 1 for SEA notification and reporting, we would like to propose using the term "promptly" or "as soon as practicable" instead of fixed timelines. This adjustment would provide the necessary flexibility while assuring you of our commitment to timely reporting.  Alternatively, we propose the following language: "the UN Partner will notify the Bank as soon as possible from the moment the credibility of the complaint has been ascertained, after any required preliminary measures have been put in place, and before the formal investigation has started".  This language ensures that victims are prioritized, that preliminary measures are effectively implemented to protect, and that accurate information is provided to you in good time. 
UNOPS prioritizes a victim-centered approach in handling SEA incidents.  Our primary focus is on the safety, well-being and confidentiality of the victims. Rigid reporting deadlines can sometimes conflict with this approach.  One can think of a complaint received on a Friday afternoon that may not be reported within a 48-hours window due to limited weekend capacity.  Initial reports often contain minimal information, sometimes only a case number without details about the alleged perpetrator or victim.  Gathering accurate preliminary information can be time-consuming, especially in remote contexts where our projects are implemented.  These challenges are not due to internal policy issues, but stem from capacity constraints in our operating environment. We hope that this solution respects both our operational realities and your need for timely information. 
I look forward to your review on this proposal. If we are aligned on the process, we can look at the language that could be added to Annex 1 to reflect this approach. 
Warm regards, 
Elizabeth

 the Bank’s corporate Grievance Redress Service (GRS).  For any other incidents or accidents, the notification and any follow up reporting to the Bank shall be shared with the Bank task team.

c)
In cases where protection concerns or applicable UN Partner rules may limit such notification or information that can be reported to the Government, the UN Partner shall promptly only notify the Bank. After
 consultations with the Bank on the modalities, extent of information to be shared and timeline of the notification to the Government of the incident or accident, notify the Government accordingly. In exceptional cases, where protection concerns outweigh the

Gentilissima, buonasera,
 
sono un funzionario diplomatico della Direzione Generale per la Cooperazione allo Sviluppo (DGCS) del MAECI. Mi ha passato
 il suo contatto il Dott. Ludovico Banova, collega dell’Ufficio Sicurezza alimentare sempre qui in DGCS.

 
Nella DGCS mi occupo, tra le altre cose, di attrazione del settore profit verso il mondo della cooperazione. Seguo pertanto
 una Fiera appositamente dedicata a realizzare questo match, denominata Codeway Expo (o semplicemente Codeway) - allego una breve scheda informativa.

 
Si tratta di un’iniziativa della Fiera di Roma cui il MAECI ha dato patrocinio, in quanto persegue gli scopi della legge
 125/2014 (legge sulla Cooperazione allo Sviluppo) ovvero innescare il coinvolgimento del settore profit nelle dinamiche di sviluppo, oltre che più semplicemente per il fatto che il MAECI promuove, per propria natura, tutti i contesti da cui possono generare
 opportunità per le imprese italiane. 
 
Nel corso della Fiera si terrà un evento dedicato al procurement e sistema di LTEs delle Nazioni Unite, in cui le imprese
 italiane potenzialmente interessate ad investire nel settore dello sviluppo potranno interloquire con gli appropriati interlocutori provenienti dal sistema ONU. Le fila di questo evento saranno tenute da UNOPS, che nei prossimi giorni ne farà circolare uno
 schema di funzionamento. Anticipo l’evento sarà in ogni caso idealmente diviso in due parti:

 

·   
una prima parte di natura seminariale, realizzata da UNOPS, dedicata a spiegare alle imprese gli strumenti e le agevolazioni per partecipare al
 procurement e LTEs onusiani.

·   
una seconda parte più interattiva dove le agenzie onusiane – in particolare, quelle presenti in Italia - effettuino presentazioni volte pubblicizzare
 le proprie opportunità (in base all’assunto che maggiore è la competizione, maggiore la qualità).

 
In proposito, saremmo davvero lieti se IFAD volesse avere un ruolo attivo in questa seconda parte. Sono chiaramente a
 sua disposizione per una telefonata - ho i suoi contatti grazie a Ludovico, ma ritenevo più corretta una prima mail di presentazione – cui seguirebbe una VTC di contatto con UNOPS e con la Fiera.
 
Grazie davvero per l’attenzione. Un cordiale saluto,
 
Filippo Lonardo

Dear George,
I hope you are well. We would like to follow up on the eligibility and report presentation of hedging gains and/or losses, as in the case of P169949 (UNOPS 21775-001) in South Sudan (Interim Financial Statement attached).
As the South Sudan project end date is approaching, we would be pleased to get your advice on how we should issue our interim and final financial reports in these cases.
Our key questions are:Are gains and/or losses from hedging transactions eligible for World Bank-financed projects? As we explained at our meeting the hedging aims to preserve the USD value of SDR-denominated projects to be able to fully deliver outputs.Is there a special consideration that we should have in our financial reporting or is the current presentation fine (hedging as a separate line under contribution)?

Thank you for your support. My colleague Megumi (supporting the Washington office from now through mid-August) would be pleased to organize a consultation with our Finance colleagues if you'd like to discuss further.
Also note that we have shared your guidance internally on the 5% contingency for SDR-denominated projects.

Subject: RE: Feeder roads proposal


 
Dear Piotr,
 
Thank you for this information. We would be definitively interested in the opportunity of accessing new funding for a feeder roads project in South Sudan. Such a project would be particularly useful for a number
 of reasons listed below. Moreover, connectivity infrastructure particularly in rural areas is something the country really needs.
 
-     
Such a project will continue and consolidate our ongoing (but soon to be completed) projects supporting feeder roads and access roads construction, in particular the one implemented by UNOPS;
-     
It will complement the activities envisaged under the new Green and Resilient Economy package (cca. EUR 80 million) that we will be contracting in the course of next year (and/or in 2025); as we want to
 focus as much as possible on boosting productivity as well as value chains, value addition, private sector development and market led growth, it is obvious that roads providing access to markets and facilitating interaction between farmers and other stakeholders
 would have a positive impact; in our current thinking for the above mentioned EUR 80 million package we would have not prioritised new feeder roads because the constructions costs are increasing and would deviate too many resources from other much needed priority
 activities; but having new funding for new feeder roads would be very useful because the needs in the country are high;
-     
As for the ongoing projects, a new project will consolidate linkages with the envisaged regional corridor 11 which is a Global gateway priority (maybe the only Global gateway related activities we can
 realistically envisage in South Sudan).
 
One important element that will greatly facilitate the success of a possible new feeder roads project is our positive relationship with UNOPS. I have discussed with the and they would be ready to engage in a
 new project should we receive the greenlight. Under our ongoing project they have built infrastructure of good quality and their work is appreciated also by the government and local authorities and communities. Initially, under the ongoing projects, some locations
 have been identified and preparations conducted, including design and review documentation produced. Yet, because the increased costs of feeder roads construction, not all the envisaged kilometres of roads could be constructed. With a new project that could
 be done rather quickly as preparatory work is already done. That could be a quick start and then new locations could be identified. Moreover, various teams of experts are already involved in the ongoing project and they could be easily and quickly transitioned
 to work under a new project.
 
UNOPS projects include to a certain extent cash for work and local workers are hired either directly by UNOPS or by contractors. Returnees could be included in such cash for work schemes and in that regard the
 project could benefit from the experience of another UNOPS implemented program on social protection that is active in Greater Bahr el-Ghazal, Upper Nile and Unity state.
 
For information, under the ongoing project, the average cost per kilometre for a 4.5 meters wide road has been 151.000 USD and for a 6 meters  wide road, including drainage structures, has been around 211.000
 USD. Most likely, the current costs would be higher, about 20% higher. Sill, if we could mobilise a substantial amount, as you indicated, ranging from EUR 20 to 50 million we could do significant work and that would be worthwhile .
 
Please let u know what are the next steps and what is expected from the Delegation (and by when). We stand ready.
 
Best regards,


Gabriel

Hi Marysia, 
While I think it is ok that we try to make the case, I would not put my money on our chances for success. 
The Danes have already provided mine clearance support to the RC Trust Fund in Ukraine and to UNDP. I would expect that they will continue to do it this way. 
Notice that the MFA has already decided that UNOPS should be a contributor to implement their goal number 8.2.2 on "Reconstruction of social infrastructure, including educational facilities, shelters, hospitals, residential areas etc. to provide basic living conditions for citizens in Mykolaiv (Mykolaiv city and oblast)".
If we are to push a bit for inclusion of our mine clearance capabilities, I would suggest doing so in connection with the reconstruction of infrastructure - pointing toward the need to clear mines and unexploded ordinances before being able to meaningfully rebuild infrastructure - and to improve living conditions for citizens.  
I would also suggest that we point towards our capability to operate not only in Mykolaiv - but throughout all of Ukraine. I definitely think that you should flag our experience in mine clearance done in connection to infrastructure and the specific mine clearing projects done for the Dutch and the French (as I recall). 
Given the current issues on the Arkas High School project, I am very concerned that the Danes are even considering our capability to do infrastructure reconstruction. I would therefore caution pushing too much on more of our capabilities - but make sure that at least they have confidence in our infrastructure capacities. 
If the meeting with Erik is online, I would be happy to join if convenient. 
In any case - it would be really good to make sure that all UNOPS participants have carefully studied the attached draft Danish programming programming for Ukraine.

Subject: Follow-up on potential collaboration with Novo Nordisk and Novo Nordisk Foundation
Body:
Dear Brian and Carolyne,
It was such a pleasure meeting with you! Thank you for taking the time to connect with us and share insights into the impactful work you are leading at Novo Nordisk Middle Africa.
As promised, I am sharing UNOPS’ health slide deck, which offers an overview of our capabilities in the health sector, along with a factsheet detailing UNOPS’ capacity within this field. 
During our discussion, we briefly touched on UNOPS' ongoing partnership with Novo Nordisk A/S. On behalf of Novo Nordisk A/S, we delivered blood transfusion equipment to Ukraine. This equipment supports a station that serves up to 40,000 patients annually. We are currently discussing a new project in Ukraine with your HQ based colleagues on providing medical equipment for several health facilities throughout Ukraine.  
I understand that challenges such as medicine storage persist in the Sahel region, particularly in Nigeria. Unfortunately, we did not have the opportunity to delve deeper into other challenges you face in the Sahel region. As I briefly mentioned, UNOPS has a strong presence in the region and specializes in operating in difficult and remote areas that are often too difficult to reach.
In our meeting, you also noted the synergies between UNOPS and the Novo Nordisk Foundation. While we would be eager to explore collaborative opportunities with the Foundation, we would also like to emphasize our interest in continuing and expanding our collaboration with Novo Nordisk A/S. Both entities offer unique opportunities to drive impactful health outcomes, and we believe there is potential to work together to achieve shared goals.
As mentioned, I would be grateful if you could connect us with your relevant colleagues from the Foundation. 
For reference, please find below a few short stories of some of the projects carried out by UNOPS in Africa. These include examples of our work in the Sahel region, as well as initiatives focused on health. 
Looking forward to hearing your thoughts and continuing our conversation.
Best regards, Asbjørn

Rehabilitating a laboratory in the DRC
In collaboration with WHO and with funding from Korea International Cooperation Agency, UNOPS reconstructed the Lubumbashi Provincial Laboratory in DRC. This included reconstructing the building, installing reliable water and electricity supplies, and procuring state-of-the-art laboratory equipment. A fully operational laboratory not only enhances disease detection and medical research but also significantly improves the quality of life for the over 2 million people in Lubumbashi, DRC. Given the country’s pressing health challenges, including measles, yellow fever, chickenpox, and other diseases, transforming this facility into a fully functional laboratory is a vital contribution to the well-being of the population
Results of the project included: Successful reconstruction of the Lubumbashi Provincial LaboratoryTraining for the local community on the operation and maintenance of the infrastructure that was builtContributed to detecting and combating communicable and noncommunicable diseases  through better diagnostic and research capabilitiesImproved the quality of life for over 2 million residents in Lubumbashi, DRC
Zimbabwe Idai recovery projectThe Zimbabwe Idai recovery  was a four-year project, where UNOPS managed a $72 million World Bank fund and worked together with UNICEF, FAO, WHO, WFP, IOM, UNFPA and UNESCO. The project aimed to build the foundations for regional recovery after Cyclone Idai hit Zimbabwe. 
Around 50,000 households were destroyed and more than 60,000 people were displaced. Nine districts faced up to $622 million in damages. The approach of this project was to help the community not just to recover what was lost - but be able to mitigate future shocks.
The results of the project include: rehabilitation of health facilities, water systems and sanitation facilities, schools, irrigation schemes, micro-watersheds and roads that connected people to services – all infrastructure that's vital to the more than 346,000 people in the impacted communities.integrated health services and gender-based violence response for more than 672,000 people, including more than 3,600 internally displaced people.local jobs, thus helping build community capacity and resilience by providing infrastructure development skills. Labor-intensive, community-focused infrastructure projects created job opportunities for more than 5,200 community members, nearly half of them women.training for local authorities on the operation and maintenance of the infrastructure that was built, ensuring it remains in good working order for communities.partners involved worked closely with Zimbabwe’s national and local government, to build stronger disaster risk governance and preparedness. This involved developing early warning and risk information systems to inform disaster risk preparedness and contingency planning.to ensure that the project laid the foundation for resilience to future shock and stresses, it involved a comprehensive climate hazard and risk assessment. It made sure to engage the local community’s views via a participatory design process. This approach informed the climate resilient and inclusive design and construction of community schools, roads, health facilities, irrigations and markets.
Powering peace and sustainable development in West AfricaOn behalf of Sweden, UNOPS is  currently bringing reliable and sustainable access to clean energy in rural areas of the Liptako-Gourma region of Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger.The project is providing access to clean and sustainable energy for over 300,000 people, and is implemented in collaboration with UNDP and the Liptako-Gourma Authority. UNOPS is responsible for the installation of 6 mini-grids – two in each country – and we are leading the development of local capacity that will ensure that the new systems can be effectively operated and maintained in the longer term. This is a three year pilot project.

We understand that an internal guidance note on the interim template usage (for all UN partners) will be distributed in the next few days to World Bank regional teams, to follow up a brief message which was shared already to World Bank country lawyers. We continue to seek a formal communication from the World Bank which UNOPS teams would be able to share with World Bank and government counterparts to reduce confusion. 
The situation remains fluid, and we will keep you updated. We appreciate your patience as we continue working with urgent projects while negotiating the permanent template. Look out for an upcoming announcement of the Sparks session on the World Bank’s Environment and Social Framework, which will occur on 26 September at 15:00 CPH.
Please don’t hesitate to reach out with any updates, questions or concerns.
Warm regards,Christine, Vinesh and Elizabeth

WLO and LG, along with relevant colleagues, will prepare a decision memo for UNOPS management, including information on the implications of the new SFA and a recommended set of internal improvements to balance the risks and opportunities posed by the enhanced ESS obligations.

On Wed, Aug 14, 2024, 8:22 AM Christine BOWERS <christinebo@unops.org> wrote:
Dear Regional Directors and Regional Partnerships Advisors,Thank you for your continued support in managing the situation following the introduction of an updated Standard Form of Agreements (SFA) by the World Bank. Please find below an update on the new requirements for UNOPS in respect to the WB Environmental and Social Framework (ESF), which I request you to carefully review. (RDs, please pay particular attention to the section on UNOPS responsibilities and associated risks.)If desired, WLO and the Technical Services Unit (Kenya MCO) would be happy to organize a 2-hour presentation on the World Bank’s Environmental and Social Framework (ESF) and discuss any bottlenecks to implementation in your region. Background: The World Bank recently posted on its website an updated framework agreement for use with UN agencies, effective 12 July 2024. Sections of this new template were not agreed/negotiated in advance with UNOPS or other UN agencies. The Bank took this unilateral action in response to urgent internal pressures on compliance with its Environmental and Social Framework (ESF) by UN agencies. UNOPS is in touch with other UN agencies on the specific language being agreed, aiming for a coordinated response where possible.While the underlying requirements of the Environmental and Social Framework have not changed, and we have largely been implementing the requested measures since they were introduced in 2018, the legal templates are being updated to more clearly outline UNOPS’ responsibilities. As communicated earlier by WLO, UNOPS has not cleared the new SFA Output and Technical Assistance templates introduced by the Bank, as our HQ-level negotiations are still ongoing. In the meantime, the WB’s Operations Policy & Country Services and UNOPS are nearing agreement on a set of interim measures to minimize the disruption to projects nearing signature.Affected Projects: This message applies to projects that are signed between UNOPS and government partners for World Bank-financed activities using the Outputs or Technical Assistance templates. We are seeking clarification on how minor amendments to existing projects will be treated.Projects using the Vehicles or Supply templates are not affected, as these agreement templates haven’t changed and remain valid. Similarly, projects receiving direct financing from the World Bank are not affected, as these agreements are individually negotiated without a template.Anticipated Interim Measures: Urgent cases—specifically, those projects listed as “approved” in the control sheet– will use the pre-existing Output or Technical Assistance templates, with the new Environmental and Social Standards (ESS) legal language incorporated. See here the current negotiation status of the language, noting that this remains draft language.For these projects, project-level WB counterparts will also be informed of these exceptional measures once finalized. These projects are expected to be signed by 31 August.Once we reach agreement with the World Bank on interim language, regional partnership advisors and focal points for affected projects will receive an email from WLO confirming the interim measures. This email will be for you to share with World Bank or government partners as needed. (The present email is for internal use.) We expect to activate the interim measures within the next day or two, depending on internal WB processes.UNOPS responsibilities and associated risks: The updated ESS provisions in the SFA require UNOPS to ensure our own compliance with the Environmental and Social Commitment Plan of projects (or similar document), as well as cascade related ESS obligations onto subcontractors and consultants via our contracts with them. We agree to ensure the capacity of these third parties to meet their ESS obligations and to monitor their compliance (and require remedial actions as needed).The newly added language on UNOPS responsibilities introduces additional legal risk exposure to UNOPS, because if there is any loss or damage to third parties, arising partly or wholly due to any failure by UNOPS to perform its ESS obligations, then UNOPS may be held responsible under the SFA to repay those losses or damages to affected third parties. 
Note also that the World Bank is requiring UNOPS to share some of our (redacted) contracts to support verification of the above. We are proposing that we receive these requests from the Bank, rather than the government, to minimize frivolous requests and reduce administrative burdens. This point is still under negotiation.
Guidance to Engagement DOA holders: Colleagues are advised to review carefully the E&S obligations contained in Annex 1 of new project agreements, with the advice of technical experts as needed, in the context of their specific engagements. Tanja Chopra in the Technical Services Unit at the Kenya MCO, has a small team which can support you with interpreting (or revising) ESS project documents if desired.
You should confirm that UNOPS has the capacity and resources to comply with those additional responsibilities before accepting the engagement. If considerable additional expertise or manpower is needed, then you may need to seek additional resources to be included in the budget. 
Engagement DOA holders are also advised to assess the additional risks that may arise from the updated E&S clauses, and identify whether any additional risk mitigation measures are necessary in the context of their specific engagements. The additional risks may be nil to minimal for engagements where there are no ESS considerations, and they may also be so considerable that it will result in the engagement no longer being acceptable to UNOPS. Next steps: As noted above, once the interim language is agreed WLO will communicate with regional partnerships advisors and affected project focal points. It will be several weeks until corporate negotiations conclude on a permanent update to the SFA templates, thus WLO will work with OPCS on a process to support projects with expected signature in September and October. WLO will continue to work through regional partnership advisors to request information and share updates.As Megumi Uchino completes her mission to the Washington Liaison Office on August 23, colleagues should direct project-level updates and requests for inclusion in the next round of interim measures to Christine Bowers. Deep appreciation goes to Vinesh Winodan, Elizabeth Duby, Megumi Uchino and Alistair Somerville for their excellent and collaborative work on this in the past weeks during my summer leave. Moving forward, I am also available for any general or specific questions related to the above. Note also that your LG colleagues are updated and will be ready to assist via the engagement tickets.I will provide a brief update once the World Bank agrees interim language for immediate use. Also I will be in touch with regional partnerships advisors about scheduling a brief session for each region with Tanja in the coming weeks.Best regards, Christine

Subject: Notes from meeting with Norway’s Embassy in Ethiopia on 12 December, 2025
Body:
Dear colleagues, 
On Friday, December 13, Asbjørn, Silke, and I met Astrid Lervåg, Head of Development Cooperation at Norway’s Embassy in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Lervåg clarified early on that no funds were currently available.
Asbjørn provided an overview of UNOPS, capacities, portfolio and key partnerships, including the World Bank, and addressed the comprehensive reforms undertaken by UNOPS since S3i. Silke presented UNOPS’ portfolio and ongoing work in eastern Africa - including a recent visit to Tigray. Lervåg emphasized the need for the population in Tigray to know and understand that the aid was coming from the central government in Addis Ababa to foster peaceful coexistence. 
Lervåg showed interest in UNOPS’ gender-based-violence (GBV) work in Tigray, indicating potential funding as the embassy felt that they had not done enough in this area. She also pointed towards Norway's ongoing support to climate adaptation/mitigation and forest preservation, carbon credits, food security, education, and human rights. Ethiopia would remain a key partner for Norway. Silke agreed to provide more information in writing ahead of a follow-up meeting that would involve the Norwegian embassy’s GBV and climate staff.  
Noting that UNOPS did not have a direct contract with Norway, Lervåg informed that Norway had provided funding via KfW which entailed the procurement of 90 vehicles - of which 30 was funded by Norway. KfW had used UNOPS for procurement and the money seemed to have disappeared without any vehicles having been delivered. Silke and Asbjørn assured Lervåg that they would follow up on the situation to clarify what had happened.
Follow-up actions: Silke  will provide more information on UNOPS’ efforts in combating GBVSilke will provide a clarification of what happened with the procurement of vehicles on behalf of KfW. Silke committed to sharing further details regarding UNOPS’ initiatives to mitigate carbon emissions.Silke will share an overview of impact figures for the work done in Tigray and as a well as a follow-up meeting in Q1                                                                            ***On Friday December 13, Asbjørn, Silke and I met with Astrid Lervåg, Head of Development Cooperation at Norway’s embassy in Ethiopia. 
Lervåg initially noted that the embassy currently had no available funding. Responding to this, Asbjørn made it clear that the intention of the meeting was merely to introduce UNOPS’ portfolio of work in Ethiopia and making the embassy aware of UNOPS’ capacities. 
Asbjørn started the meeting by providing an overview of UNOPS, noting that the World Bank is UNOPS’ biggest partner. He also addressed the comprehensive reforms of UNOPS following S3i and current positive relations at HQ level between UNOPS and Norway. Silke provided an overview of UNOPS Africa and the Ethiopia Multicountry Office. 
Lervåg noted that she had recently attended The Development Partners Group meeting, where UNOPS provided a great presentation on its work in the Tigray region. Lervåg asked if UNOPS could be helpful in providing impact figures for the work done in Tigray, which Silke confirmed. Lervåg also pointed toward the need to ensure that the government of Ethiopia was sufficiently credited for the project to help facilitate the sensitive relationship between the population in Tigray and the federal government in Addis. 
Silke noted that the efforts in remote areas affected by the conflict was important and highly appreciated by the local population, which could be testified by the recent visit. Asbjørn informed that UNOPS’ projects were mainly driven by local colleagues who very well understood the sensitive context and how appreciative and emotional the local community was during the recent handover of one of the schools. Asbjørn further informed that the community also very well appreciated the local contractors as well as stones, woods and equipment used to build the schools.  
Lervåg appreciated the impressions and suggested a common site visit in the future to see the impact of UNOPS’ projects - which Silke confirmed that she would be happy to organise. 
Lervåg expressed particular interest in the combating gender-based violence (GBV) component of the Tigray portfolio, acknowledging that the embassy had not yet done enough in this area. She mentioned that GBV was an area where the embassy could be interested in providing funding. In response, Silke promised to follow up with more details on UNOPS’ efforts to combat GBV, particularly highlighting the infrastructure aspect and UNOPS’ capacity to build safehouses.
Noting that UNOPS does not have a formal contract with Norway, Lervåg informed about an agreement with KfW which entailed the procurement of 90 vehicles - of which 30 was funded by Norway. According to Lervåg, KfW had used UNOPS for procurement and the money unfortunately seemed to have gotten lost. She expressed confidence that KfW would resolve the issue but mentioned that it remains unresolved as of now. Silke and Asbjørn assured that they would look into the matter and follow up asap.    Lervåg informed that after Ukraine, Ethiopia was Norway’s second second-largest partner - with a particular focus on climate and forest. Specific areas of collaboration included:
Carbon Credit: Supporting Ethiopia’s ambition to establish carbon credit initiatives, with UNDP serving as the procurement partner and FAO as the monitoring partner.Food Security: Working with the government and NGOs to advance climate-smart agriculture.
Lervåg noted that the resilience component in the Tigray portfolio was an interesting opportunity for Norway. Silke promised to follow up with more information on UNOPS’ efforts to reduce carbon emissions. 
Lastly, Lervåg highlighted that Norway provided funding within education through the World bank and UNICEF’s education in emergencies, where focus was on capacity building of teachers. Silke and Asbjørn complemented the work done by UNICEF and UNDP and pointed towards the need to also provide infrastructure in the education sector, which UNOPS was uniquely positioned to deliver - which Lervåg took notice of.   
Best, Naimo

Subject: Notes from meeting with Finland’s embassy to Ethiopia, 12 December, 2025
Body:
Dear Colleagues,
On December 12, Silke, Asbjørn, and I met Pia Korpinen, Education Counsellor at the Embassy of Finland to Ethiopia, and her colleague, Worke.
Ms. Korpinen was only familiar with UNOPS’ capacity for procurement due to a World Bank-funded program supported by Finland. She knew UNOPS as a contractor and for what had happened with S3i in Helsinki. Asbjørn provided an overview of UNOPS’ mandate, capabilities, and the comprehensive and transparent reforms of UNOPS since S3i. 
Ms. Korpinen informed that Finland’s country strategy for Ethiopia (2021-2024) had been extended to include 2025. While there would likely be an increased focus on the possibilities of generating bilateral trade, Finland’s development priorities in Ethiopia would likely remain focused on education and WASH.
Silke outlined potential collaboration opportunities, particularly in education and WASH, highlighting UNOPS’ work in Tigray and areas where Finland could provide support such as school kitchens and WASH systems that could complement work already done by UNOPS. A follow-up meeting in January 2025 was agreed based on more written information about UNOPS’ projects and capacities. 
Ms. Korpinen expressed appreciation for the outreach and noted that Finnish colleagues did not have a clear understanding of UNOPS’ very tangible and impactful work. Silke and Asbjørn emphasized UNOPS’ significant presence in Ethiopia, with a portfolio of USD 120-150 million supporting key ministries.
Follow-up: Silke will provide further information on UNOPS’ WASH projects in Ethiopia and arrange for a follow-up meeting.

                                                                         ***
On 12 December 2025 Silke, Asbjørn, and I had the opportunity to meet Pia Korpinen, Education Counsellor at the Embassy of Finland to Ethiopia, who was accompanied by her colleague, Worke.
Ms. Korpinen mentioned her awareness of UNOPS, recognizing its role in procurement and its involvement in a World Bank-funded program supported by Finland.
Asbjørn provided an overview of UNOPS, including its mandate and capabilities. He also addressed the S3i situation, outlining the comprehensive response plan and current relations between UNOPS and the Finnish government. Ms. Korpinen acknowledged her familiarity with S3i but noticed that it had been handled in a comprehensive and transparent way. 
Ms. Korpinen shared insights of Finland’s country strategy for Ethiopia 2021-2024 which had been extended by one year. The process of negotiations with government counterparts was expected to begin in 2025 and Finland is expecting changes within its strategy in 2025 as the strategy has overall been the same for many years. She informed that the strategy would likely shift towards the key guidelines published last year and that we should expect a lighter version in 2026. Given the timing for adjusting the Finnish strategy, it was therefore timely to get introduced to UNOPS’ impactful and tangible work in Ethiopia with a view of considering potential collaboration. 
M.s Korpinen noted that Ville Tavio, Minister for Development and Foreign trade visited Ethiopia in June 2024, highlighting an increased emphasis on trade. However, Finland’s focus areas for development cooperation in Ethiopia are expected to remain unchanged:  
Education A World Bank-led sector program (procurement partly outsourced to UNOPS) starting in 2025, with a reduced annual budget from $600M to $200M. Education in emergencies, where UNICEF was one of the key partnersTechnical assistance in education with emphasis on inclusive education Digitalization initiatives, beginning in early 2025 in collaboration with the EU 
WASH - celebrated 30 years of community WASH collaboration in Ethiopia Bilateral collaboration with 7 regionsContribution to the ONEWASH national program.   
PIF: A programme that was a combination of grants and loans in four regions. The programme had taken a long time to develop and would be a way to try to mobilise private funding via an agreement between Finnish companies, the ministry of finance and the government of Finland.
Silke noted that there might be synergies in collaborating within education and WASH, due to UNOPS’ extensive work in Tigray - funded by the World Bank. A lot of the ground work, prioritisation of sites, etc. had already been done - which made it possible for partners like Finland to rapidly engage with quick, tangible results. Silke provided concrete examples for opportunities for school kitchen and WASH systems. Silke and Ms. Korpinen agreed that this would be followed up by a meeting in January 2025 based on more written information. 
Asbjørn informed that the World Bank was UNOPS largest partner and that UNOPS was the World Bank's largest implementing partner in fragile countries. Asbjørn further asked how Finland intended to combine trade with development in the Ethiopian context. Pia acknowledged that it is not an easy exercise and that there was no financial gain in the education sector. 
Silke elaborated about UNOPS’ Ethiopia portfolio of about 120-150 million USD and on UNOPS’  support to the ministries of finance, health and agriculture. 
Ms. Korpinen informed that many of her colleagues did not have a good understanding of what UNOPS was doing and delivering on behalf of partners like the World Bank - to which Finland provided funding. She informed that Finland collaborated with the same Ministries and that she got little information about the impact of the work funded by Finland. Silke and Asbjørn offered to provide written information on the impact of the work done by UNOPS - to showcase examples of the tangible effects Follow-up: Silke will provide a follow up on UNOPS presence in Ethiopia and work within the WASH and educational sector - as well as written information about UNOPS’ capacities on procurement and infrastructure. 
Best regards, Naimo

Dear Sophia,
Happy 2025! 
It was an absolute pleasure meeting you before the Christmas break! Thank you for taking the time to connect with us and share insights about the critical work you do in Kenya.
With our expertise in infrastructure, procurement, and fund management, UNOPS could be uniquely positioned to manage the FCDO initiative supporting Kenyan SMEs. Our already existing framework agreement with the UK streamlines the process for signing an agreement, eliminating the need for a lengthy tender process - should you chose UNOPS. This allows you to focus on strategic priorities rather than administrative tasks.
Since 2010, UNOPS has successfully delivered Fund Management services on behalf of governments and multilateral organizations, including the FCDO, managing nearly $2 billion. Our tailored solutions aim to maximize impact while minimizing risks, ensuring confidence in achieving tangible results.
As my colleagues Fumie and Sharon mentioned, they are keen to meet with you and your team covering Sudan and Somalia to explore opportunities for collaboration at your earliest convenience. 
As promised, I have highlighted examples of Fund Management support that UNOPS has provided for the FCDO. Please also find below a few short stories about some of the projects carried out by UNOPS in Africa. I believe that these initiatives align with your strategic goals in peace and security, climate resilience, health, education, and humanitarian assistance.
Examples of Fund management support that UNOPS has provided for the FCDO
Strengthening Humanitarian Preparedness and Response Programme (SHPR)From 2016 - 2021, UNOPS managed the programme: Strengthening Humanitarian Preparedness and Response Programme (SHPR) in Bangladesh. This project received a total funding of $203 million, and provided support to UK-funded actors in Bangladesh. UNOPS performed fund management services, providing oversight, fiduciary management. monitoring and evaluation, as well as the design of an emergency recovery facility. The programme has supported nearly one million Rohingya refugees through scaling up health services, WASH, and education, alongside strengthening the national response to natural disasters.
Modernisation and Improvement of Policing ProjectThe programme aimed to improve security and justice service provision for the poor and traditionally excluded communities in Nepal. The programme received a total funding of $33 million. The objectives of the programme was to change social barriers that impede access to justice, increase engagement among communities and security and justice institutions for better prevention of crime and insecurity and Improved response to criminal violence through improved capabilities and performance of security and justice institutions.
The Local Assistance Myanmar Programme (LAMP)This programme is the UK's response in Myanmar through the Humanitarian and Resilience Programme. This programme has so far received a total funding of $61 million The programme was previously managed by Crown Agent. The objective of this programme is for highly vulnerable people in the most conflict affected areas to receive prioritised assistance and protection, primarily from empowered and representative national and Civil Society Organisations (CSOs).The results of the programme include: Delivery of multi-sectoral humanitarian assistance for Rakhine, Shan and Kachin State through provision of grants to CSOs and local or international NGOs (I/NGOs), including capacity building activities for local partners and support to local partner coordination mechanisms.Development of MHAP strategy as part of Programme inceptionEstablishment of framework for monitoring, learning, evidence and knowledge management.

Examples of projects carried out by UNOPS in AfricaPowering peace and sustainable development in West Africa
On behalf of Sweden, UNOPS is bringing reliable and sustainable access to clean energy in rural areas of the Liptako-Gourma region of Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger.The project is providing access to clean and sustainable energy for over 300,000 people, and is implemented in collaboration with UNDP and the Liptako-Gourma Authority. UNOPS is responsible for the installation of 6 mini-grids – two in each country – and we are leading the development of local capacity that will ensure that the new systems can be effectively operated and maintained in the longer term. This is a three year pilot project.

The project aimed to build the foundations for regional recovery after Cyclone Idai hit Zimbabwe.

This approach informed the climate resilient and inclusive design and construction of community schools, roads, health facilities, irrigations and markets.

This includes water, sanitation and solid waste systems, roads and electricity supply. UNOPS has rehabilitated more than 230 kilometers of roads in 8 cities and restored access to critical services for more than 3 million people. 4. Support to Tunisia’s border control and management of migration flowsFunded by the Italian government, this project aims at supporting Tunisian authorities in the continued and improved control of maritime borders by enhancing operational capacities of the fast patrol fleet of the maritime National Guard.

Dear Aslak, 
Wishing you a happy 2025!
It was an absolute pleasure meeting you and once again thank you so much for welcoming me at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. 
I wanted to kindly follow-up on our recent discussion regarding the proposal focused on developing technical and financing models to maximize access to solar energy and energy-efficient cooling solutions in the date and dairy value chains across five areas in Tunisia. For reference, please find attached the proposal as well as an overview of UNOPS’ presence in North Africa. 
To summarise, the proposal focuses on enhancing access to solar energy and energy-efficient cooling solutions in Tunisia's date and dairy value chains. It aims to develop technical and financing models that will benefit over 3,000 farmers, fostering sustainable livelihoods and addressing root causes for migration. Agriculture contributes 10% to Tunisia’s GDP and employs 16% of the workforce, with dates accounting for 12% of the total value of agricultural exports. The proposal is developed in collaboration with UNEP and incorporates a multi-donor funding model, making it easy for Denmark to take part in together with other partners. 
As we discussed, there is much alignment between this project and the DAPP priorities; climate action, youth employment, and migration. 
In the meeting, I also noted that Denmark could potentially be interested in supporting initiatives such as these projects carried out by UNOPS on behalf of our partners in Tunisia: Support to Tunisia's Border Control and Management of Migration Flows (Italy),  Support for Maritime Border Management (EU), and Procurement Service Project for land border control (Italy). Adding additional support to successful and well-established projects offers significant value for money for Denmark. 
My colleagues Claudia, Asbjørn and I would very much appreciate a virtual meeting with your team and relevant colleagues at MIGSTAB in week 2 or 4 to explore these collaboration opportunities. Could you kindly let us know when this might work for you? 
Best regards,Naimo

Dear Agnes and Sally,
A late - but very happy new year to both of you! I hope you have had a chance to enjoy some offline time with your loved ones. 
As usual I wanted to provide you with a brief overview of the topics relevant for UNOPS at the upcoming EB session on January 27-31. I am sorry that I am a bit late with this overview, as we already have the first informal session this afternoon at 5 pm CET about the status of the Comprehensive Response Plan and UNOPS' digitalisation plan (the so-called PID). 
I am sure that you have already seen that all the relevant documents were uploaded to the website here - but I just wanted to share the link with you to gather all the pieces in one email. 
I was wondering if perhaps you would have time to briefly catch up in advance of the EB - to get your initial take on the topics and for me to perhaps clarify matters, point towards (for us) important aspects, etc. If so - please just let me know when it might suit you. 
Further to the topics to be discussed at the upcoming EB, I have provided you with a quick overview of the upcoming informal session below for your ease of reference. 13 January: The comprehensive response plan and the UNOPS report on the Process Innovation and Digitalization Programme implementation 14 January: Informal consultation with UNDP, UNFPA, UNOPS on the joint update on organization culture 17 January: Joint UNDP, UNFPA, UNOPS orientation for the Executive Board (our DED Sonja will give an introductory presentation on UNOPS to the EB members)20 January: Briefing on undisbursed excess reserves, with UNBOA 21 January: Joint consultation on enterprise risk management 22 January: Joint informal with JIU on JIU report on governance and oversight There will also be two closed session during the EB week:28 January: Closed briefing on S3i funds recovery, with OLA30 January: Closed briefing on portfolio risk assessment  Topics to be discussed at the EB relevant to UNOPSUNOPS' response to the recommendations of the UN Board of Auditors for 2023The UNBOA report for 2023 on UNOPS was unqualified (also known as "clean") - meaning that our financial statements are deemed to present a true and fair view of UNOPS' financial position and performance, comply with UN accounting standards and are free of material misstatements. UNBOA issued 9 recommendations classified as high priority and 10 recommendations classified as medium priority.  The implementation of all recommendations is on track for completion within the timelines. Because the recommendations were issued in July 2024, and many of them require long-term attention, UNOPS will need to work beyond 2024 to implement them all successfully.In the implementation schedule UNOPS is targeting an implementation rate of 68% during the 2024 audit cycle, which will surpass that of 2023 (58%). 

Governance and oversight functions of the Executive Board At the last EB session the Bureau was tasked to develop a terms of reference for the operationalisation of a working group to review the 31 recommendations of the Joint Inspection Unit (JIU) and to develop actions for their implementation. In advance of the last EB session in 2024, UNOPS developed this informal document outlining UNOPS' views on the JIU recommendations. The document also contains the views of the ethics offices of the involved agencies. 

Risk managementAt the last EB session, UNDP, UNFPA and UNOPS were asked to provide updates on the agencies' efforts to improve the enterprise risk management system and inform the EB of any critical risks of strategic importance. From a UNOPS perspective The joint information note points towards key risks associated with project delivery, financial management and stakeholder engagement. It also points to more concrete risks regarding UNOPS' operations in fragile and conflict affected places, shortage of talent, sexual abuse due to the geographical operations of UNOPS, regaining trust among partners since S3i failures, implementing the many reforms at UNOPS and increasing financial constraints.     

Organisational cultureThe informal information note provides an update on the implementation of the work plan to transform the organisational culture. Status of each action point is in this annex.    

Implementation of the Comprehensive Response PlanThis is the last update to the EB on the implementation of the CRP. As the note was written in November, 3 of the outstanding recommendations were yet to be completed by the end of 2024. These related to 1) revising the management and organisational culture towards broader engagement and less top-down, 2) invest in outcome-reporting, and 3) revision of financial rules and regulations.  The EB is asked to release the third tranche (11.8M USD) for the implementation and to initiate the second independent review of the implementation of the CRP.  

Review of the whistleblower processThe informal information note provides an overview of the now completed overhaul of UNOPS' whistleblower mechanism. The new system is set to launch in January 2025 and will introduce: 1) a central platform for reporting, 2) ressources to provide early informal guidance, 3) a workplace conduct team within PLG, 4) a new advisory group to address systemic issues. 

Portfolio risk assessment of UNOPSAs a response to the original KPMG recommendations a portfolio risk assessment is presented that outlines a number of risks in UNOPS' portfolio. These relate e.g. to 1) challenges in managing complex infrastructure projects, 2) large-scale procurement of health products, 3) capacity of supplivers and implementing partners. 

Calculation method for excess reservesThe note presents a suggestion for revising the calculation methodology for calculating UNOPS' excess reserves. The proposed changes are to ensure that only liquid assets are calculated as part of the potential excess reserves and that only if the excess reserve exceeds 20% of the minimum operational reserve, it should trigger the refund process. By the end of 2023 UNOPS distributed 123.2M USD of the excess reserve back to partners and all other funds had been transferred to the RC system and the SDG fund. Only 0.6M USD is withheld as these relate to discussions with partners. 

Implementation of the PIDThis is the annual status of implementation of the PID that points towards progress in seven programmes (country engagements, partnerships and project management, procurement, HR, finance, data, market research for the new ERP). Notice that the selection of a new ERP system can only be done after a formal evaluation is presented to the EB (as requested by the EB). Therefore the timeline for the PID has been extended by one year to 2028.I hope this brief overview helps - and I look very much forward to hearing your initial thinking about the topics. 
All the best,Asbjørn--

Subject: Dokumenter til kommende EB
Body:
Kære Rikke og kolleger på Asiatisk Plads, 
Et sent - men rigtig godt nytår til jer alle! Jeg håber, I har haft mulighed for at nyde noget offline tid med dine kære. 
Som vanlig ville jeg give jer et kort overblik over de emner, der er relevante for UNOPS på den kommende EB-session den 27.-31. januar. Jeg beklager at den kommer noget sent, da vi allerede i eftermiddag kl. 17 har den første uformelle session om status for Responsplanen og UNOPS’ digitalisering (den såkaldte PID). 
I har sikkert allerede bemærket, at alle de relevante dokumenter er uploadet til hjemmesiden her - men hermed også for at samle alle brikkerne i én e-mail. 
Jeg forstår, at Danmark igen er medlem af bestyrelsen - men antager at den kommende session dækkes af jeres FN-mission? Under alle omstændigheder ville jeg sætte stor pris på. om I havde tid til at mødes kort, mhp. en uformel drøftelse om de vigtigste emner på dagsordenen. Kunne det fx passe at mødes i UM på fredag d. 17. ved 14-tiden? 
Ud over overblikket over de emner, der skal drøftes i bestyrelsen ultimo januar, har jeg nedenfor givet et hurtigt overblik over de kommende uformelle sessioner 13 januar: Status på Responsplanen og UNOPS’ digitaliseringsprogram (PID) 14 januar: Fælles møde med UNDP, UNFPA og UNOPS om organisationskultur 17 januar: Fælles UNDP, UNFPA, UNOPS orientering for nye medlemmer (vores DED Sonja vil holde et oplæg om UNOPS)20 januar: Briefing om ikke-udbetalte overskydende reserver, med UNBOA 21 januar: Risikostyring, sammen med UNDP og UNFPA 22 januar: Uformel, fælles dialog med JIU om JIU-rapport om styring og tilsyn Der vil også være to lukkede sessioner i løbet af EB-ugen:28 januar: Lukket briefing om inddrivelse af S3i-midler med OLA30 januar: Lukket orientering om porteføljerisikovurdering  Emner, der skal diskuteres på EB, der er relevante for UNOPSUNOPS' svar på anbefalingerne fra FN's Revisionsråd for 2023UNBOA-rapporten for 2023 om UNOPS var ukvalificeret (eller "ren") - hvilket betyder, at vores regnskaber anses for at give et retvisende billede af UNOPS' finansielle stilling og resultater, overholder FN's regnskabsstandarder og er fri for væsentlige fejl. UNBOA udsendte 9 anbefalinger klassificeret som høj prioritet og 10 anbefalinger klassificeret som medium prioritet. Implementeringen af alle anbefalinger er på sporet med forudset færdiggørelse inden for tidsfristerne. I implementeringsplanen sigter vi efter en implementeringsgrad på 68% i løbet af 2024-revisionscyklussen, hvilket vil være lidt højere end i 2023 (58%).

Bestyrelsens ledelses- og tilsynsfunktioner Ved den sidste EB-session fik Præsidiet til opgave at udvikle et kommissorium for operationalisering af en arbejdsgruppe at gennemgå 31 anbefalinger fra Joint Inspection Unit (JIU) og at udarbejde konkrete handlingspunkter. Forud for den sidste EB-session i 2024 udviklede UNOPS dette uformelle dokument, der skitserer UNOPS' synspunkter om JIU-anbefalingerne. Dokumentet indeholder også synspunkter fra de involverede agenturers etikkontorer. 

RisikostyringVed den sidste EB-session blev UNDP, UNFPA og UNOPS bedt om at give opdateringer om agenturernes bestræbelser på at forbedre risikostyring og informere EB om eventuelle kritiske risici af strategisk betydning. Fra et UNOPS perspektiv peges i det fælles informationsnotat på bl.a. risici forbundet med projektlevering, økonomistyring og interessentengagement. Der peges også på mere konkrete risici vedrørende UNOPS' operationer i skrøbelige og konfliktramte steder, seksuelt misbrug på grund af UNOPS' geografiske operationer, genvinding af tillid blandt partnere siden S3i, implementering af de mange reformer hos UNOPS og tiltagende økonomiske begrænsninger.     

OrganisationskulturDet uformelle informationsnotat giver en opdatering om implementeringen af arbejdsplanen for at transformere organisationskulturen. Status for hvert handlingspunkt findes i dette bilag.    

Implementering af responsplanenDette er den sidste opdatering om implementeringen af CRP. Da notatet blev udarbejdet i november, var 3 af de udestående anbefalinger endnu ikke afsluttet ved udgangen af 2024. Disse vedrørte 1) revision af ledelses- og organisationskulturen mod bredere engagement og mindre top-down, 2) investering i resultat- rapportering, og 3) revision af finansielle regler og forskrifter. Disse er nu implementeret. EB anmodes om at godkende frigivelsen tredje tranche (11,8 mio. USD) til implementeringen og at indlede den anden uafhængige gennemgang af implementeringen af CRP.  

Gennemgang af whistleblower-processenInformationsnotatet giver et overblik over det nu afsluttede eftersyn af UNOPS' whistleblower-mekanisme. Det nye system skal lanceres i januar 2025 og vil introducere: 1) en central platform til rapportering, 2) ressourcer til at give tidlig uformel vejledning, 3) et team for adfærd på arbejdspladsen og 4) en ny rådgivende gruppe til at håndtere systemiske problemstillinger. 

Porteføljerisikovurdering af UNOPSSom et svar på de oprindelige KPMG-anbefalinger er udarbejdet en porteføljerisikovurdering der skitserer en række risici i UNOPS' portefølje. Disse vedrører f.eks. 1) udfordringer i styring af komplekse infrastrukturprojekter, 2) storstilet indkøb af sundhedsprodukter og 3) kapacitet hos leverandører og implementeringspartnere. Hertil kommer naturligvis det faktum, at hovedparten af UNOPS’ aktiviteter foregår i konfliktramte og volatile områder. 

Beregningsmetode for overskudsreserverNoten præsenterer et forslag til revision af beregningsmetoden til beregning af UNOPS' overskydende reserver. De foreslåede ændringer skal sikre, at kun likvide aktiver beregnes som en del af de potentielle overskydende reserver, og at tilbagebetalingsprocessen kun udløses hvis den overskydende reserve overstiger 20 % af den minimale operationelle reserve. Ved udgangen af 2023 distribuerede UNOPS 123,2 mio. USD af den overskydende reserve tilbage til partnere, og alle andre midler var blevet overført til RC-systemet og SDG-fonden. 0,6 mio. USD tilbageholdes, da disse vedrører igangværende drøftelser med partnere. 

Implementering af digitaliseringsprogrammet - PIDDette er den årlige status for implementering af PID, der peger mod fremskridt i syv programmer (landeengagementer, partnerskaber og projektledelse, indkøb, HR, økonomi, data, markedsundersøgelser for den nye ERP). Bemærk, at valget af et nyt ERP-system kun kan foretages, efter at en formel evaluering er præsenteret for EB (som anmodet af EB). Derfor er tidslinjen for PID blevet forlænget med et år til 2028.Jeg håber, at denne korte oversigt hjælper - og jeg ser meget frem til at høre jeres indledende tanker om emnerne.

Jeg vil ikke selv være tilstede under EB - da jeg er i Oslo til NORAD konferencen. Hvis I har tid til at mødes til en frokost, kaffe eller lignende, ville det være super. Jeg rækker ud særskilt herom.
