Subject: Notes from ED meeting with Danish State Secretary, Elsebeth Søndergaard Krone on May 2
Body:
On May 2 the ED met with the newly appointed Danish State Secretary for Development, Ms. Elsebeth Søndergaard Krone who had formally assumed her position the day before. 
The State Secretary accepted an invitation by the ED to soon visit the UN City and meet the UNCT Country team.
The State Secretary was pleased to engage in conversations on how to deal with the implementation gap - a topic that should be discussed at the upcoming Copenhagen Dialogue, tentatively planned for October. Although this was a topic of the greatest interest to the Danish government, the State Secretary pointed to the extraordinarily busy time with the Danish EU Presidency and membership of the Security Council.
The State Secretary thanked for the "incredible" work done on behalf of Denmark in Ukraine. She had already seen some of the projects and looked forward to seeing even more results on the ground. The ED pointed towards the potential for expanded collaboration in Africa, to which the State Secretary responded that fund allocations were done locally at the individual embassies in Africa, whereas in Ukraine it was done centrally from Copenhagen. She therefore urged local UNOPS colleagues to approach the respective Danish embassies. 
Finally the State Secretary looked very much forward to the gathering of the CEB. It would be a testament to the reestablished confidence in UNOPS - and the Danish government would continue to support UNOPS wherever possible.       
***  The State Secretary initially assured the ED that the Danish government was committed to stick to 0.7% ODA in their new development aid strategy - despite internal pressure on shifting funds away from development towards military spending. The government was determined to invest in both peace and defence. 
The ED complimented the Danish government's approach - noting that Denmark had been one of the few countries that has consistently and historically defended human rights, set ambitious climate targets and provided at least 0.7% of GNI in ODA. Also in light of this, it was positive that the CEB would gather in Denmark. The ED thanked for Denmark's support during the S3i crisis and for helping in getting the CEB to gather in Denmark. 
The ED pointed towards UNOPS being able to showcase the very tangible results of ODA funding - especially in fragile and conflict affected areas. The ED also invited the State Secretary to visit the UN City, the humanitarian warehouse and to meet the UNCT Country Team. 
Upon inquiries from the State Secretary the ED explained the circumstances surrounding the S3i revelations, the comprehensive response plan, the ongoing transformational initiatives and the aspiration for a growing UNOPS as demand was increasing. 
The State Secretary urged the ED to share UNOPS reform experiences with other UN entities - as it could serve as a role model for potential upcoming reforms. The State Secretary looked forward to upcoming dialogue about a broader reform of the UN in relation to UN80. Talks about reforming the UN had been ongoing for decades, but the US funding cut had created a burning platform which necessitated a more efficient UN with less overlapping mandates, better sharing of services, etc. It was a key message from the Danish government, that all UN agencies should stick to their respective mandates. 
The ED informed about UNOPS next strategic plan for 2026-29 where the underlying theme was the need to scale up and speed up - which would also encompass doing things more efficiently. The ED also explained that UNOPS would be mission-driven, but not programmatic. It would mean that UNOPS should not accept all projects and be ready to deliver on the 8 missions. UNOPS would also move away from measuring output to outcomes. 
Finally the State Secretary pointed towards the fact that at every COP there was an enormous pressure for more funding. As a consequence far too many different funds had been set up - with great absorption difficulties. The process of implementation was far too slow and results on the ground were not visible fast enough. 
The State Secretary considered if a sort of one-shop UN access point for delegating tasks might be a way of delegating tasks among UN entities - and avoiding overlapping tasks/mandates. 
In confidence the State Secretary mentioned that she found that far too often UNDP had accepted projects that UNDP did not have the capacities to fulfill. 
Best,Asbjørn

Subject: Notes from informal meeting with Danish MFA ahead of the Annual EB session, June 2-5
Body:
Dear colleagues, 
This morning I briefly met informally with the working level at the Danish MFA, who is preparing the Danish position for the upcoming Annual EB session. 
While the Danes noted that they did not yet study all the documents for the EB session, they offered their help and support if there were particular issues important to UNOPS.  I noted their kind offer and pointed towards our desire for the EB to 1) acknowledge the closure of the Comprehensive Response Plan, 2) unlock funding for the implementation of the PID and 3) endorse UNOPS' approach to the next Strategic Plan, noting that UNOPS would not venture into new territories and stick to the original mandate as set out in Resolution 65/176 and subsequent EB decisions. 
The Danes underlined that - like many other Member States - it would continue to be a key priority for Denmark to ensure that UNOPS would stick to its mandate of providing infrastructure, procurement and project management.  I assured the Danes that this would be the core message of the next Strategic Plan - while we would also work towards more outcome (rather than only output) based reporting and become mission driven to ensure a return to UN values.   
As for the independent third party review of the implementation of the CRP, the Danes noted the importance of maintaining momentum on aspects related to culture, as this was a key concern for many Member States. 
The Danes were also keen on hearing UNOPS' views on the UN80  discussions. I referred to the statement given by the SG yesterday and noted that we would be pleased to continue to work on the implementation capacity of partners - both the UN and other partners. Subject: Notes from informal meeting with the FCDO ahead of the Annual EB session, June 2-5
Body:
Dear colleagues, 
Yesterday afternoon I met informally with working level FCDO colleagues to informally discuss key topics at the upcoming Annual EB session. 
The current UNOPS focal point at FCDO HQ and EB member, Ms. Agnes Annells will be leaving by the end of May to assume the position as Deputy Ambassador in Kosovo. Agnes will be temporarily replaced by Ms. Emily Boyce at FCDO HQ who will attend the Annual EB session. Kavoy Ashley will remain the UNOPS focal point at the UK Mission in NYC. 
Upon request the FCDO confirmed that it was still the intention to conduct a Strategic Dialogue with UNOPS after the spending review had been completed. 
Strategic Plans and UN80The FCDO considered that the Annual EB session would be clouded by UN80 as this was the talk of town and the main focus of most WEOG members. They considered it an unfortunate timing to be discussing Strategic Plans when everyone was considering much wider efficiency reforms of the entire UN system. The UN80 might not affect UNOPS as profoundly as some of the other agencies and UN bodies - but there would still be a Member State focus on ensuring a more efficient UN throughout the discussions about the strategic plans. 
The UK would - like other Member States - continue to mention that UNOPS should stick to its original mandate, and deliver in fragile and conflict affected places. The UK also looked forward to seeing what comparative advantages UNOPS would present. Finally the UK advised that UNOPS somehow made sure to frame how the Strategic Plan would address the writing on the wall - namely a more efficient UN in view of declining funding. 
PIDThe UK expected a focus on the request to release funds for the PID at the EB session. Some Member States would likely not accept the release of funds before the identified risks had been addressed. I Referenced that these would be addressed in the forthcoming management response. 
EthicsThe development of ethics and a culture turnaround in UNOPS would continue to be a focus area for the UK. 
It was difficult for the EB members to handle the series of anonymous letters being sent to the Board. From a UK perspective, the key was to ensure a proper process for handling the complaints and restoring trust in UNOPS' ability to handle these matters internally via the proper channels - such as the whistleblower system. 
AccountabilityFinally the UK noted that there seemed to be a renewed interest among some members for the recent media attention towards the former ED having been questioned by the FBI. 

/Asbjørn

--

Dear William,



I would like to give you some feedback on our attempt today, May 21, 2025, to officially submit the building permit application for the prison.



Unfortunately, things didn't go as planned. The building permit department was unable to process the application, claiming they had no knowledge of the project or of UNOPS. This project requires special attention from VROMI and cannot be handled as an ordinary
 project, due to its sensitivity and the confidential nature of the documents. As a result, the official submission of the application could not take place. One example of the issues encountered concerns certain supporting documents that are required, but not
 applicable since the request comes from one minister to another.



Progress is therefore nonexistent at this stage. A meeting is now being organized (coordinated by Johishi) with VROMI, MinJu, the Fire Department, CSI, and UNOPS, in order to officially present the project and clarify everyone’s responsibilities. It is worth

Despite this, we are taking this episode as a lesson and are now moving towards a more structured coordination through this meeting.



I wanted to inform you of this incident, as I found the attitude of the VROMI building department inappropriate and clearly uncooperative. 


 


This is even more regrettable as it goes against previous discussions held with SG Plaisimond and Minister Gumbs, which were intended to streamline the process and support the progress of the project.

Dear Katerina,Thank you always for your very quick reply and for your suggestion to approach your regional MENA team in Amman. Could I kindly ask for your suggestion on who I should reach out to? In the meantime I will suggest our Tunisia team (Claudia - cc this email) to touch base with your colleague Roger from the Swedish Embassy in Tunis.For your background information, UNOPS is currently delivering projects for $180 million in Tunisia, Morocco, Algeria and Libya on behalf of our partners. Our efforts in the region primarily focus on strengthening land and border control, maritime border management, counter terrorism etc., which might be of interest for Sweden.To further maximize impact on the region’s challenges with migration, we are looking at a Nordic multidonor approach on migration management, where we are not only looking at direct border control but also building local capacity and infrastructure for re-integration of returnees as well as communities vulnerable to migration.This initiative will address not only direct border control but also vital areas such as re-integration infrastructure, support for communities vulnerable to migration, and resources for returnees.Finally, to clarify your question on who is the “demandeur” of the project, this is with the respective program countries - e.g. Tunisia, Algeria, Morocco, Libya, etc. in this case. The projects are co-developed among beneficiaries, donors and UNOPS as the middle man. I hope this clarifies. Beyond migration, UNOPS has a significant presence in Northern Africa, covering areas such as health, private sector development, sustainable energy, climate and environmental action, and institutional capacity building. For this purpose, my colleagues from UNOPS Tunisia Office would like to connect with the SIDA Regional MENA team in Amman.Best regards, Naimo

Subject: New EU Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) presented to the EP (2028-2034)
Body:
Dear colleagues,Last wednesday the European Commission presented its proposal for an ambitious and dynamic long-term EU budget, the so-called Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), which will run for seven years, starting in 2028. Almost €2 trillion, or 1.26% of the average EU's gross national income between 2028 and 2034, will support Europe’s ambition to be independent, safe, prosperous and thrive over the coming decade.Europe faces an increasing number of challenges in numerous areas such as security, defence, competitiveness, migration, energy and climate resilience. These reflect systemic geopolitical and economic shifts that require a strong and forward-looking response.  The Commission therefore proposes a fundamental redesign of the EU budget, which will be more streamlined, flexible and impactful. It will significantly enhance the EU's capacity to deliver on core policies, while addressing new and emerging priorities. This budget will continue to support people, business, Member States, regions, partners, and - above all - the EU's collective future. While the modalities have been highly criticised by the European Parliament  and not only (apparently President Von der Leyen did not share the text until a few days ago and the text seems to have been drafted by a very tiny group of people) I thought it would be interesting to share with all of you the numbers that are on the table and that concern our work (external action).Heading 3 - Global Europe, which includes  the Common Foreign and Security Policy and Overseas Countries and Territories (including Greenland) amounts to EUR 215.2 billion.What we know for now on the geographic distribution is:Candidates/accession countries will receive €42 billion.The largest share is intended for Sub-Saharan African countries, with nearly €60 billion, North African and Middle Eastern countries, with €42 billion. These are the regions from which funds will be drawn to finance agreements with third countries aimed at curbing migrant departures or increasing returns. Ukraine is treated separately. Ursula von der Leyen has announced €100 billion for resilience and reconstruction. However, the resources are expected to remain outside the budget and flow into the “Ukraine Facility,” likely through a new loan program guaranteed by the EU.

Please note that this is still to be approved unanimously by the EU Council of Ministers and then to be given the consent by the European Parliament, but it gives you an idea on which direction the budget is taking.
I will be happy to answer any question you may have

Subject: Informal conversation with Denmark on Executive Board and other matters
Body:
Dear colleagues, 
Earlier today I met with the Deputy Director for the Multilateral Department, the UN team as well as the Deputy Director for the Financial Control Department at the Danish MFA to informally discuss the upcoming Executive Board and other topics. 
The Danish MFA praised the collaboration with UNOPS - noting the recent successful CEB in Copenhagen, common efforts to increase awareness about the UN and UNOPS in Denmark, engagements in Ukraine, Afghanistan, Santiago Network, Somalia, etc. and UNOPS' unique ability to showcase tangible results of the UN work in difficult circumstances.  
I conveyed our key messages on the 4 key topics ahead of the August EB, noting that the Danes had not yet studied the vast amount of documents provided by UNOPS and the other UN agencies in advance of the EB. The MFA pointed towards the information overload to be an increasing worry that they had hoped could be solved in relation to the JIU recommendations - although they did not have much confidence in the process. 
The Danish MFA would no longer allocate as many internal resources to follow UNOPS EB matters, as they considered the issues following the S3i revelations to be closed and as they did not allocate core contributions to UNOPS. Formally the matter would be closed by a report from the MFA to the Danish Court of Auditors in the coming months. 
The Danish focus would henceforth be on the specific projects/engagements (which they expected to increase) and on a global perspective on UNOPS risk management and the KPMG follow-up recommendations in relation to EB matters. The MFA Financial Control Division would therefore be at leading the Danish engagements in EB matters. 
It was noted that the government continued to receive a number of parliamentary questions relating to UNOPS (UNBOA recommendations on the inappropriate use of financial hedging instruments, DUNDEX, status on recovering missing S3i funds, etc.).   
Denmark would continue to attend EB sessions due to UNOPS being headquartered in Copenhagen and would seek to act as a goodwill ambassador for UNOPS - although not being at the forefront of the WEOG group. 
In general Denmark was supportive of the UNOPS Strategic Plan - praising the efforts to ensure that UNOPS would stick to the core mandate and work towards being better at measuring outcome better rather than only output. However, Denmark noted that UNOPS was a very output based organisation producing very tangible results, which UNOPS should not shy away from as it remained one of the strongest competencies / selling points of UNOPS.  
Denmark was aware of the critical voices within the WEOG group of UNOPS Mission Hubs - but found that EB Members had understood that this was merely UNOPS internal knowledge sharing hubs. Denmark - and other WEOG members - did however continue to find the term "mission" unfortunate as it had an unfortunate link to "normative". 
Denmark found it unlikely that the EB would approve UNOPS' full request to allocate additional 60M USD from the reserves to the PID as this was a very large amount of funds over a long period of time to a very large IT project. The Danes considered it more likely with partial allocations of funds during the time period - with regular reporting to the EB. UNOPS was encouraged to develop a plan B - containing solid arguments for how much funding allocation was strictly needed for now to ensure predictability in planning - while additional funding could be allocated at a later period.
Finally it was agreed to initiate drafting of a standard template for engagements between Denmark and UNOPS to ease the workload in the negotiation process for colleagues and as there was an increasing amount of engagements between Denmark and UNOPS. 
Best,Asbjørn
